Brief Review

Retired lawman Wyatt Earp tries to start a new life in the mining town of Tombstone only to be forced out of retirement.

Story

Wyatt Earp (Kurt Russell) arrives at the train station with his two brothers Virgil (Sam Elliott) and Morgan (Bill Paxton) and meet up with their wives before making the trek to the mining town of Tombstone. Wanting to start a new life far away his past as a lawman. Unfortunately, the people of Tombstone know of him and his reputation. They were made aware of the presence of a gang that tries to run the town, known as the cowboys. One night, one of the cowboys, while drunk, started shooting randomly in the middle of town. The sheriff tried to calm him down and arrest him for the night until he could sober up, but instead got shot. Virgil decided that there has to be some law and order and picked up the badge at the behest of Wyatt. But, the lawlessness became too much and Earp brothers, with the help of long time friend Doc Holliday (Val Kilmer) tried to bring justice to the streets of Tombstone.

What was good

I loved every minute of this movie. You learned really early on the kind of character Wyatt Earp is, demanding and intimidating but with a heart for doing what is right. Someone that has a vicious bark and an even more devastating bite. But only shows it off when truly needed. I also loved Val Kilmer's portrayal of Doc Holliday. He had a level of elegance and sophistication that most people in that time didn't have. I don't what else I can say here. I thoroughly enjoyed this movie. And I also thought it was a good touch to see how Allie (Wyatt's Wife, Paula Malcomson) slowly developed an opium addiction that started to ruin her life. It was a little thing that you rarely see come from hollywood (the dangers of degeneracy).

What was bad

While I loved this movie, there was one thing that was bad that caused a ripple effect of some other issues. While the movie clocks in at 2 hours, I don't think that was enough time. They could have easily made this 30 minutes longer and have extended many segments. For example, there is a montage scene when Wyatt and his band go after the cowboys. I would have preferred to see them actually go after them, like a scene when they sneak up to a small shack somewhere to kill the cowboys, or running into them in town and chasing them on horseback to gun them down. More, is what I'm saying. While the montage section was good, I would have liked more exposition. And also, there were two death scenes that suffered from needing more time, too. Without spoiling it, they both died right as Wyatt walked away. Like, Wyatt was there just at the right time to ease their suffering. With more time, they could have drawn them out some and make them more impactful. And one small gripe, I'm not a fan of opening and closing narration to give some backstory. While I understand that sometimes it's needed to lay the ground work for what's about to happen, again, with more time, they could have put more scenes in to show the viewer what happened that lead up to this moment.

Final Thoughts

This movie came out in 1993 and at that time in my life, I was not a fan of westerns. Now, having watched it, I'm kicking myself for not watching it sooner. This was a great throwback to when films were not political propaganda to the level they are today.

If you enjoy westerns, this is a must own. Even if you apathetic to the environment of a movie, it's a great story with memorable characters. I think the only people who won't like it are those with a hardon hatred of westerns.

Oath of Office

In the Federal Government, in order for an official to take office, he or she must first take the oath of office; this is also known as a swearing-in ceremony. The official reciting the oath swears an allegiance to uphold the Constitution. The Constitution only specifies an oath of office for the President; however, Article VI of the Constitution states that other officials, including members of Congress, "shall be bound by Oath or Affirmation to support this constitution."

Executive Branch:

President

"I do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will faithfully execute the office of President of the United States, and will to the best of my ability, preserve, protect and defend the Constitution of the United States."

The Vice President

"I do solemnly swear that I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic, that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same: that I take this obligation freely, without any mental reservation or purpose of evasion, and I will well and faithfully discharge the duties of the office on which I am about to enter. So help me God."

Senate Oath of Office

I do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will support and defend the Constitution of the United States against all enemies, foreign and domestic; that I will bear true faith and allegiance to the same; that I take this obligation freely, without any mental reservation or purpose of evasion; and that I will well and faithfully discharge the duties of the office on which I am about to enter: So help me God.

Judicial Branch: Supreme Court Justices

According to Title 28, Chapter I, Part 453 of the United States Code, each Supreme Court Justice takes the following oath:

"I, [NAME], do solemnly swear (or affirm) that I will administer justice without respect to persons, and do equal right to the poor and to the rich, and that I will faithfully and impartially discharge and perform all the duties incumbent upon me as [TITLE] under the Constitution and laws of the United States.
